title: A Two-Phase Deep Learning Framework for Adaptive Time-Stepping in High-Speed Flow Modeling
claim: A two-stage system predicts the step size, then advances the state by it, in training and in autoregressive rollout.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; training left, rollout right, timeline with dashed arrows
description: The figure has two rounded gray panels. The left panel, "Training", has dashed beige Inputs and Targets boxes on either side of a lavender ShockCast box. The Inputs box holds a ground-truth flow-field heatmap u(t) and a gray Ground Truth Δt pill. The ShockCast box holds Neural CFL (ψ) and Neural Solver (φ) blocks. Arrows lead from the inputs through these blocks to a Target Δt pill and a predicted u(t+Δt) heatmap. The right panel, "Autoregressive Rollout", has a time axis labeled "Adaptive Time-Stepping" with uneven tick marks. Dashed arrows run from the ticks to three viridis-colored blast-wave snapshots. Between consecutive snapshots, a Neural CFL block outputs a predicted Δt, which feeds a Neural Solver block. The eye goes first to the colorful heatmaps and the lavender blocks.
caption: Overview of the ShockCast framework for time-adaptive modeling of high-speed flows. Left: Training pipeline. The neural CFL model and time-conditioned neural solver are conditioned on the current flow state and predict the corresponding timestep size ∆t and flow state ∆t ahead, respectively. Right: Inference pipeline. ShockCast autoregressively alternates between predicting the timestep size given the current flow state using the neural CFL model and evolving the flow state forward in time by the predicted timestep size using the neural solver model. Note that the example data are from the circular blast dataset we generated in this work.
abstract: We consider the problem of modeling high-speed flows using machine learning methods. While most prior studies focus on low-speed fluid flows in which uniform time-stepping is practical, flows approaching and exceeding the speed of sound exhibit sudden changes such as shock waves. In such cases, it is essential to use adaptive time-stepping methods to allow a temporal resolution sufficient to resolve these phenomena while simultaneously balancing computational costs. Here, we propose a two-phase machine learning method, known as ShockCast, to model high-speed flows with adaptive time-stepping. In the first phase, we propose to employ a machine learning model to predict the timestep size. In the second phase, the predicted timestep is used as an input along with the current fluid fields to advance the system state by the predicted timestep. We explore several physically-motivated components for timestep prediction and introduce timestep conditioning strategies inspired by neural ODE and Mixture of Experts. We evaluate our methods by generating three supersonic flow datasets, available at https://huggingface.co/divelab. Our code is publicly available as part of the AIRS library (https://github.com/divelab/AIRS).
